source_title: The DEPRE'5 study: pragmatic, multicentre, five-arm, parallel-group randomised controlled trial with blinded assessment to compare treatment strategies in major depression after a failed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a five-arm, blinded-assessment randomized controlled trial (DEPRE'5, EudraCT No. 2007-002130-11), MDD patients unresponsive to an initial SSRI achieved higher response rates and greater depressive-symptom-severity reduction with alternative second-line strategies (lithium augmentation, nortriptyline combination, switching to venlafaxine, or adding problem-solving therapy) than with simple SSRI dose optimization.
population: 257 adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) unresponsive to an initial SSRI, randomized across 5 arms: SSRI dose optimization (n=51), lithium augmentation (n=46), nortriptyline combination (n=48), switch to venlafaxine (n=55), and SSRI plus problem-solving therapy (n=57).
intervention: Four alternative second-line strategies after SSRI non-response: lithium augmentation, nortriptyline combination, switching to venlafaxine (an SNRI), or adding problem-solving therapy to the existing SSRI.
comparator: SSRI dose optimization (continuing/increasing the dose of the original SSRI).
outcome: Week-6 response and remission rates (primary), assessed by blinded evaluators using the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-17); change in HDRS-17 score (secondary).
result_summary: Pooled across the four alternative strategies, response was higher than with SSRI dose optimization (28.2% vs 14.3%; odds ratio 2.36, 95% CI [1.0, 5.6], p=0.05), with greater HDRS-17 score reduction (-2.6 points, 95% CI [-4.9, -0.4], p=0.021). Remission was numerically higher but not statistically significant (16.9% vs 12.2%; OR 1.46, 95% CI [0.57, 3.71], p=0.27). Individually, switching to venlafaxine (OR 2.53, 95% CI [0.94, 6.80], p=0.067; HDRS-17 difference -2.7, 95% CI [-5.5, 0.0], p=0.054) and SSRI-plus-problem-solving-therapy (OR 2.46, 95% CI [0.92, 6.62], p=0.074; HDRS-17 difference -3.1, 95% CI [-5.8, -0.3], p=0.032) showed the most consistent effects among the four alternative arms.

source_span.locator_note: The response/remission odds ratios and HDRS-17 differences this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Alternative second-line strategies led to higher response (28.2% v. 14.3%, odds ratio = 2.36 [95% CI 1.0-5.6], p = 0.05) ... with greater HDRS-17 score reductions (-2.6 [95% CI -4.9 to -0.4], p = 0.021]) than SSRI-Opt.
limitations: The trial's own conclusion notes 'limited statistical power'; several individual-arm comparisons (e.g. venlafaxine's response-rate OR, both alternative arms' remission effects) reached only marginal or non-significance (p=0.05-0.27).

The five arms are not all pharmacologically comparable (one arm adds psychotherapy rather than a medication change), so this record's pooled 'alternative strategies vs SSRI-Opt' comparison combines heterogeneous intervention types.
This is a second-line (post-SSRI-failure) population, not treatment-naive MDD patients, so results should not be generalized to first-line SSRI/SNRI efficacy.
Nortriptyline combination showed the most adverse effects (75% vs 28.1% in SSRI+PST, p<0.01), a safety trade-off this record's efficacy-focused summary does not fully capture.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the abstract reports.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question by addressing a specific, clinically important subpopulation: patients who have already failed an SSRI. It directly supports the venlafaxine (SNRI) switch strategy specifically with real HDRS-17 data, and should be read alongside first-line SSRI/SNRI efficacy records in this corpus rather than as a general statement about SSRI/SNRI efficacy from treatment initiation.

source_title: Escitalopram versus other antidepressive agents for major depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: A meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials found escitalopram significantly more effective than citalopram (another SSRI) for acute response and remission in major depressive disorder, though escitalopram did not differ significantly from other antidepressants in early or follow-up response.
population: Adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) enrolled in 30 randomized controlled trials comparing escitalopram against another antidepressant (16 trials vs another SSRI, 14 trials vs a newer antidepressant), identified via search of Medline/PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and ClinicalTrials.gov through July 2023.
intervention: Escitalopram (SSRI).
comparator: Other antidepressants, including citalopram (another SSRI) and other newer antidepressant agents.
outcome: Acute-phase treatment response and remission, calculated on an intention-to-treat basis; risk ratios (dichotomous data) and standardized mean differences (continuous data) with 95% confidence intervals, random-effects model.
result_summary: Escitalopram was significantly more effective than citalopram in achieving acute response (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI [0.50, 0.87]) and remission (risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI [0.30, 0.93]). No significant difference was found between escitalopram and other antidepressants in early response or follow-up response to treatment.

source_span.locator_note: The escitalopram-vs-citalopram risk ratios this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Escitalopram was shown to be significantly more effective than citalopram in achieving acute response (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50-0.87). Escitalopram was also more effective than citalopram in terms of remission (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30-0.93).
limitations: The headline statistically significant finding is specific to the escitalopram-vs-citalopram comparison (both SSRIs); the abstract explicitly states no significant difference was found between escitalopram and other (non-citalopram) antidepressants in early or follow-up response.
This record does not independently assess the meta-analysis's heterogeneity statistics, publication-bias assessment, or risk-of-bias grading across the 30 included trials.

The direction of the reported risk ratios (both <1, described in the source as favoring escitalopram) reflects the paper's own reported outcome framing (e.g. risk of non-response/non-remission); this record reports the values and the paper's own stated direction rather than independently re-deriving the RR's numerator/denominator definition.
This is a manual extraction from one systematic review/meta-analysis only, not an independent reanalysis of the 30 underlying trials.
The comparator category 'other antidepressants' pools multiple distinct agents and drug classes, which may have differing individual effects obscured by the pooled non-citalopram comparison.
uncertainty_notes: This record directly supports the corpus's core question by summarizing 30 randomized trials of an SSRI's comparative efficacy. It should be interpreted alongside individual trial records and other comparative-efficacy meta-analyses in this corpus, given the pooled, cross-trial nature of a meta-analytic estimate.

source_title: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing the Effects of Vilazodone, Escitalopram, and Vortioxetine Monotherapy on Metabolic Parameters in Patients With Major Depressive Disorder
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a three-arm randomized controlled trial, vilazodone, escitalopram (an SSRI), and vortioxetine monotherapy each substantially reduced depressive symptom severity over 16 weeks in adults with major depressive disorder, including those with comorbid type 2 diabetes, with no statistically significant between-drug difference in the degree of symptom reduction.
population: 96 adults with major depressive disorder who completed a 16-week, three-arm, randomized, open-label trial (of 134 screened, 119 eligible, 96 in the per-protocol population); mean age 46.3 +/- 6.2 years; stratified into diabetic and non-diabetic subgroups. Registered in the Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI/2022/07/043808).
intervention: Vilazodone (20-40 mg/day) or vortioxetine (5-20 mg/day) monotherapy.
comparator: Escitalopram (10-20 mg/day, an SSRI), used as the active control arm.
outcome: Change in 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-17) score from baseline to 16 weeks; metabolic indices (fasting blood sugar, HbA1c, lipid profile, hepatic parameters, serum creatinine) as secondary outcomes.
result_summary: Median baseline HDRS score was 30.0 across all three groups (p=0.964, no significant baseline difference). At 16 weeks, median HDRS scores had dropped to 15.0 (vilazodone), 14.0 (escitalopram), and 13.0 (vortioxetine). Post hoc analysis showed no statistically significant between-group differences in HDRS reduction or in most metabolic parameters, except for reductions in glycemic indices specifically among diabetic patients.

source_span.locator_note: The baseline and 16-week HDRS scores this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Across all study groups, the median baseline HDRS score was 30.0 (p = 0.964). At 16 weeks, the equivalent scores dropped to 15.0, 14.0, and 13.0 (p = 0.002)... The post hoc analysis manifested no statistically significant changes between any parameters.
limitations: Open-label design (not blinded), which can inflate apparent symptom improvement relative to placebo-controlled or blinded trials.
Small per-arm sample size (approximately 32 per arm within the 96-patient per-protocol population), limiting power to detect true between-drug differences.

The abstract's p=0.002 figure is ambiguous as extracted -- it is not fully clear from the abstract text alone whether this refers to the within-group change over time or a between-group comparison at 16 weeks; this record reports the values as stated without resolving that ambiguity, and notes the abstract's own explicit statement that post hoc analysis found no significant between-group differences.
This record does not independently assess dropout/attrition patterns (23 of 119 eligible participants did not complete the per-protocol population) or their potential effect on the reported results.
This is a single trial from a single registry region (India); generalizability to other populations is not independently assessed here.
uncertainty_notes: This record directly supports the corpus's core question with real HDRS-17 symptom-severity data for escitalopram (an SSRI), while also providing head-to-head context against vilazodone and vortioxetine (non-SSRI/SNRI serotonergic agents) and diabetes-comorbidity context. The apparent large within-arm symptom reduction (HDRS ~30 to ~13-15) should not be read as isolating drug effect from open-label/regression-to-the-mean effects, which this uncontrolled-for-placebo design cannot rule out.

source_title: Agomelatine as adjunctive therapy with SSRIs or SNRIs for major depressive disorder: a multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In an 8-week, multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adding agomelatine to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment did not significantly improve depressive-symptom reduction, remission, or response over adding placebo, in MDD patients with inadequate SSRI/SNRI response.
population: 123 adults with MDD who had an inadequate response to SSRI or SNRI treatment lasting at least 2 weeks; 60 randomized to agomelatine augmentation, 63 to placebo augmentation, both added to continued SSRI/SNRI treatment.
intervention: Agomelatine added to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment.
comparator: Placebo added to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment.
outcome: Primary: HAMD-17 total score at week 8. Secondary: HAMD-17 at weeks 2 and 4, remission and response rates over 8 weeks, self-rated depression/anxiety/anhedonia/sleep/social/cognitive functioning, and adverse events.
result_summary: The between-group difference in HAMD-17 reduction from baseline to week 8 was not significant (adjusted difference in means -0.12, 95% CI [-3.94, 3.70], p=0.90, Cohen's d=-0.022). Remission occurred in 30/60 (50.0%) of the agomelatine group vs 33/63 (52.3%) of the placebo group (OR 0.88, 95% CI [0.42, 1.85], p=0.74). Response occurred in 36/60 (60.0%) vs 41/63 (65.2%) (OR 0.85, 95% CI [0.40, 1.80], p=0.68). No secondary outcome (HAMD-17 at weeks 2/4, PHQ-9, HAMA, GAD-7, CGI severity, SHAPS, SDS, or cognitive-function measures) reached statistical significance between groups. Agomelatine was generally well tolerated with a safety profile comparable to placebo.

source_span.section: Table 2 (Primary outcomes, secondary outcomes and safety)
source_span.locator_note: The HAMD-17 adjusted mean difference and the remission/response counts and odds ratios this record centers on appear in Table 2 on page 8 of the local PDF; the null top-line result is also stated in the structured Abstract's Results/Conclusions on page 1.

short_source_excerpt: HAMD-17 at week 8: Agomelatine+SSRI/SNRI 7.2 (5.2), n=60; Placebo+SSRI/SNRI 7.4 (6.3), n=63; adjusted difference in means -0.12 (-3.94 to 3.70), p=0.90. Response: 36 (60.0%) vs 41 (65.2%), OR 0.85 (0.40-1.80).
limitations: This is an augmentation-trial population (SSRI/SNRI non-responders), not treatment-naive MDD patients, so the null result speaks to agomelatine add-on value specifically, not to SSRI/SNRI first-line efficacy itself.

A null result on the primary endpoint does not establish that agomelatine augmentation is ineffective for all subgroups; the trial was powered (80% power, Cohen's d=0.52) for a medium effect size, so smaller true effects could be missed.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports.
The trial evaluates agomelatine as an adjunct, not SSRI/SNRI monotherapy, so it is evidence about augmentation strategy choice, not about the base SSRI/SNRI treatment's own efficacy.
uncertainty_notes: This record is a genuine negative/null RCT result and is included specifically for that reason: it should be read alongside this corpus's positive-result records (e.g. DEPRE'5's venlafaxine-switch and SSRI+PST arms) as evidence that not every second-line augmentation strategy after SSRI/SNRI non-response shows benefit -- agomelatine augmentation did not, in this trial.

source_title: The safety and efficacy of escitalopram and sertraline in post-stroke depression: a randomized controlled trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a randomized controlled trial in post-stroke depression (PSD) patients, escitalopram produced greater depressive-symptom reduction than sertraline, with a faster onset of effect and a lower incidence of adverse effects, though overall response rate did not differ significantly between the two SSRIs.
population: 60 adults (aged 40-89) with an ICD-10 diagnosis of post-stroke depression (PSD), randomized 1:1 to escitalopram (n=30) or sertraline (n=30), registered as ChiCTR1800017373.
intervention: Escitalopram, flexibly dosed 10-20 mg/day, titrated over 2 weeks.
comparator: Sertraline, flexibly dosed 50-200 mg/day, titrated over 2 weeks.
outcome: HAMD-24 and HAMA-14 scores at baseline and 1, 3, 4, 6, and 8 weeks; overall response rate (>=50% HAMD-24 reduction); adverse-effect incidence (via TESS); cognitive function (MOCA) and daily-living ability (ADL) at 8 weeks.
result_summary: HAMD-24 scores decreased significantly in both groups over the 8-week follow-up, with a statistically significant between-group difference favoring escitalopram (F=4.068, p<0.05); the difference was already significant at the end of week 1 (T=2.620, p<0.05), indicating faster onset. HAMA-14 anxiety scores decreased in both groups with no significant between-group difference (F=3.185, p>0.05). Overall response rate did not differ significantly between groups (chi-squared=3.042, p>0.05). Adverse-effect incidence was significantly lower in the escitalopram group (chi-squared=9.097, p<0.05). Cognitive function (MOCA, Z=1.040, p>0.05) and daily-living recovery (ADL, Z=0.143, p>0.05) improved comparably between groups.

source_span.section: Results (Comparison of HAMD-24/HAMA-14 scores; Clinical efficacy; Adverse effects)
source_span.locator_note: The F-statistics, p-values, and chi-squared test results this record centers on appear in the body-text Results section on pages 4-5 of the local PDF; the paper does not report raw per-group response-rate percentages in extractable text, only the significance tests.

short_source_excerpt: escitalopram showed superior efficacy in alleviating depression symptoms compared to sertraline (F = 4.068, p < 0.05)... the overall response rate showed no significance between the TC and CG, while the incidence of adverse effects was lower in patients receiving escitalopram intervention.
limitations: Small sample size (n=30 per arm) from a single center, explicitly flagged by the authors as needing replication in larger cohorts.

Population is specifically post-stroke depression in an older cohort (median age ~67), a comorbid population, not general-population MDD -- findings should not be generalized to first-line SSRI choice outside this context without caution.

The paper reports significance tests (F, T, chi-squared statistics and p-values) rather than raw per-group response-rate percentages in the extractable text, limiting the precision of this record's effect-size reporting.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports; 2 patients per arm withdrew before completion.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question with a head-to-head SSRI-vs-SSRI comparison (escitalopram vs sertraline) in a specific comorbid population (post-stroke depression), rather than either drug vs placebo. It should be read as evidence for relative within-class efficacy/tolerability differences, not as a general statement that SSRIs as a class outperform or underperform SNRIs.

source_title: Antidepressants available in Japan for older people with major depressive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a systematic review and pairwise meta-analysis of double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of antidepressants available in Japan (including the SSRIs escitalopram and sertraline, and the SNRI venlafaxine, among others) for older adults with MDD, antidepressants as a class significantly outperformed placebo on response and symptom-severity improvement, but were also associated with significantly higher discontinuation due to adverse events.
population: Older adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) enrolled across 9 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials (n=2,145 total); no trial was conducted in Japan, but all evaluated antidepressants available in the Japanese market.
intervention: Antidepressants available in Japan, including duloxetine, escitalopram, imipramine, sertraline, venlafaxine, and vortioxetine.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Response rate (primary), depressive symptom scale score improvement, remission rate, all-cause discontinuation, discontinuation due to adverse events, and incidence of at least one adverse event.
result_summary: Antidepressants had significantly higher response rates than placebo (RR 1.38, 95% CI [1.04, 1.83], p=0.02) and significantly greater improvement in depressive symptom scale scores (SMD -0.62, 95% CI [-0.92, -0.33], p<0.0001). However, antidepressants were associated with significantly higher discontinuation due to adverse events (RR 1.94, 95% CI [1.30, 2.88], p=0.001) and a significantly higher incidence of at least one adverse event (RR 1.11, 95% CI [1.02, 1.21], p=0.02) versus placebo. Groups did not differ significantly on remission rate or all-cause discontinuation. The authors concluded antidepressants available in Japan are only weakly recommended for moderate-to-severe MDD in older adults, given the efficacy-tolerability trade-off.

source_span.locator_note: The response-rate, symptom-improvement, and discontinuation risk ratios this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Antidepressants have significantly higher response rates than placebo (RR [95% CI] = 1.38 [1.04, 1.83], p = 0.02)... antidepressants were associated with a higher discontinuation rate due to adverse events (RR [95% CI] = 1.94 [1.30, 2.88], p = 0.001).
limitations: Population is specifically older adults (age criteria vary by included trial), an age-restricted subgroup, not general-population MDD -- findings should not be generalized to younger adult SSRI/SNRI efficacy without caution.

The meta-analysis pools multiple distinct antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRI, TCA, and others) rather than isolating SSRI/SNRI-specific effects, so the pooled response-rate and discontinuation risk ratios should not be attributed to any single agent or class without checking the paper's per-drug subgroup analyses.

Only 9 trials (n=2,145) were available for this older-adult population, a comparatively small evidence base for a meta-analysis, which the authors' own conclusion ('only weakly recommended') reflects.
This record does not independently assess the meta-analysis's study-selection criteria, heterogeneity statistics, or publication-bias assessment beyond what the abstract reports.
uncertainty_notes: This record supports the corpus's core question at the class level (antidepressants including SSRIs/SNRIs reduce depressive symptoms more than placebo) while also surfacing a real efficacy-tolerability trade-off in older adults specifically -- it should be read as evidence-synthesis-level support with an important population-specific caveat, not as an unqualified endorsement.

source_title: Efficacy and safety of aticaprant, a kappa receptor antagonist, adjunctive to oral SSRI/SNRI antidepressant in major depressive disorder: results of a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adding aticaprant (a kappa opioid receptor antagonist) to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment produced a significantly greater reduction in depressive symptoms than adding placebo, in MDD patients with an inadequate response to their SSRI/SNRI.
population: 184 adults (18-64) with moderate-to-severe MDD (MADRS >= 25) and inadequate response to an ongoing antidepressant for 6 weeks to 12 months; 169 included in safety analyses (aticaprant n=85, placebo n=84), 166 in full intent-to-treat efficacy analyses, and 121 placebo lead-in non-responders in the enriched intent-to-treat analysis.
intervention: Aticaprant 10 mg once daily, added to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment, for 6 weeks.
comparator: Placebo added to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment.
outcome: MADRS (Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale) total score change from baseline at week 6; treatment-emergent adverse events.
result_summary: Aticaprant significantly improved MADRS total score versus placebo at week 6 in both analysis populations: enriched intent-to-treat (least squares mean difference -2.1, upper limit 1-sided 80% CI -1.09, 1-sided p=0.044, effect size 0.23) and full intent-to-treat (-3.1, upper limit 2.21, 1-sided p=0.002, effect size 0.36). The between-group difference was larger among participants with higher baseline anhedonia (Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale score >= baseline median). Most common treatment-emergent adverse events for aticaprant vs placebo were headache (11.8% vs 7.1%), diarrhea (8.2% vs 2.4%), nasopharyngitis (5.9% vs 2.4%), and pruritus (5.9% vs 0%); discontinuation due to adverse events was low and similar between arms (1.2% each).

source_title: Efficacy of empagliflozin as adjunctive therapy to citalopram in major depressive disorder: a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In an 8-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adding empagliflozin to citalopram produced significantly greater improvement in depressive symptom severity than adding placebo to citalopram, in outpatients with moderate-to-severe MDD.
population: 90 outpatients (age 18-60) with moderate-to-severe depression (HDRS >= 17), medication-free for at least the prior 2 months, randomized to placebo+citalopram or empagliflozin+citalopram.
intervention: Empagliflozin 10 mg daily, added to citalopram 40 mg daily.
comparator: Placebo, added to citalopram 40 mg daily.
outcome: Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) score at weeks 0, 4, and 8.
result_summary: HDRS scores in the placebo+citalopram group were 28.42 (SD 3.83), 20.20 (SD 3.82), and 13.42 (SD 3.42) at weeks 0, 4, and 8 respectively. In the empagliflozin+citalopram group, HDRS scores were 27.36 (SD 3.77), 13.76 (SD 1.40), and 7.00 (SD 1.13) at the same timepoints. Using repeated-measures ANOVA, the empagliflozin group showed significantly greater improvement in depression severity over time than the placebo group (p=0.0001).

source_span.locator_note: The per-week HDRS means, SDs, and the repeated-measures ANOVA p-value this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: HDRS scores were equal to 28.42(+/-3.83), 20.20(+/-3.82), and 13.42(+/-3.42) in the placebo group... These scores were 27.36(+/-3.77), 13.76(+/-1.40), and 7.00(+/-1.13), respectively, for the group treated with empagliflozin... (p value = 0.0001).
limitations: This is an augmentation-trial design (empagliflozin added to citalopram in both arms), so the result speaks to empagliflozin add-on value specifically, not to citalopram/SSRI monotherapy efficacy in isolation (both arms received an active SSRI).
Single-center trial with a comparatively small sample (n=90) and the authors' own conclusion explicitly calls for larger, longer-follow-up replication.

Empagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor (a diabetes medication) being repurposed for a neuromodulating/anti-inflammatory rationale -- this is off-label adjunct evidence, not evidence about SSRI/SNRI mechanism itself.

source_title: The effect of escitalopram in treating mild to moderate depressive disorder and improving the quality of life in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting - a double-blind randomized clinical trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a double-blind RCT in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) with comorbid mild-to-moderate depression, escitalopram significantly reduced depression scores and significantly improved quality of life compared to placebo.
population: 50 patients undergoing CABG at Tehran Heart Hospital (Jan-May 2021) with mild-to-moderate depression, randomly assigned to escitalopram or placebo.
intervention: Escitalopram, assessed at 4 and 8 weeks after treatment.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Depression severity via Beck's Depression Inventory; quality-of-life status and domains via the SF-36 questionnaire, at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks.
result_summary: No significant between-group difference existed at baseline in depression level (p=0.312) or quality of life (p=0.607). Escitalopram significantly reduced depression scores at weeks 4 and 8 compared to placebo (p<0.001). Quality of life and its domains were significantly higher in the escitalopram group at 8 weeks post-treatment compared to placebo.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 87 patients

diagnosed with depression at The Third People’s Hospital of Tianshui over a 2-year period were retrospectively analyzed. Intervention: Group A (n = 43) received only escitalopram,

while group B (n = 44) received a combination of escitalopram and Naoan dropping pills for a period of 2 months. Comparator: This was quantified as <50% reduction

in the HAMD score compared to baseline, along with stag-

nant or unimproved hemodynamic indices. Outcome: Cerebral hemodynamics were

evaluated using transcranial Doppler ultrasound (TCD).
claim_text:
There were no statistical differences between

the 2 groups in terms of age, gender, education duration, BMI,

and disease course, between the group A and the group B

(P > .05).

In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 87 patients

diagnosed with depression at The Third People’s Hospital of Tianshui over a 2-year period were retrospectively analyzed. Intervention: Group A (n = 43) received only escitalopram,

while group B (n = 44) received a combination of escitalopram and Naoan dropping pills for a period of 2 months. Comparator: This was quantified as <50% reduction

in the HAMD score compared to baseline, along with stag-

nant or unimproved hemodynamic indices. Outcome: Cerebral hemodynamics were

evaluated using transcranial Doppler ultrasound (TCD).
claim_text:
Comparison of efficacy between the 2 groups

This retrospective analysis showed that, based on HAMD

scores recorded after treatment, the effective rate in Group B

was 90.91% (40/44), which was higher than that of Group A

at 72.09% (31/43).

source_title: Trazodone effectiveness in depression: impacts of trazodone extended release vs SSRIs on the health status and quality of life of patients with major depressive disorder.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Data were gathered from 180 subjects through a naturalistic

observation

study

of

trazodone

effectiveness

in

depression

(TED)

and

analyzed. Intervention: The TED study participants received trazodone XR of SSRIs in

ﬂexible doses for 12 weeks. Comparator: At baseline, the subjects treated with trazodone XR vs SSRIs presented

similar health status proﬁles and HRQoL values with respect to the mobility, self-

care, and anxiety/depression dimensions along with lower scores for the usual

activities, pain/discomfort, overall HRQoL, and health status. Outcome: The health status and health-related quality of life

(HRQoL) were evaluated using the EQ-5D-5L tool at baseline as well as 2, 4, 8,

and 12 weeks.
claim_text:
Compared to SSRIs, trazodone XR provided greater

improvements in terms of the self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and

anxiety/depression measures and more often improved participant overall health

status and HRQoL.

source_title: Prediction of depression treatment outcome from multimodal data: a CAN-BIND-1 report.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: In the CAN-BIND-1 dataset of 192 adults with MDD and outcomes of treatment

with escitalopram, we applied machine learning models in a nested cross-validation frame-

work. Intervention: The present study uses data from the first 8

weeks when all participants received escitalopram as a monother-

apy. Comparator: A combination of baseline tier 1 clinical, neuroimaging, and molecular variables pre-

dicted response with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.57 (best model mean 0.62) compared to

0.54 (best model mean 0.61) in single modality models. Outcome: Since we aimed to index improvement in a

way that is independent of baseline severity (Kennedy et al.,

2012), we chose response, defined as a reduction in MADRS by

50% or more from baseline to week 8, as the primary outcome

measure.
claim_text:
Using a single predictor modality led to

a mean accuracy of 0.542 (95% CI 0.541–0.543; S.E. = 0.000562),

the combination of two predictor modalities predicted a mean

accuracy of 0.553 (95% CI 0.552–0.554; S.E. = 0.000597), the com-

bination of features across all three modalities predicted response

with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.573 across methods (95% CI

0.571–0.575; S.E. = 0.000971).
